utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Case IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Gaynor, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? I do understand that the next witness would be Witness 031, to be examined through videolink, with protective measures: Face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Before we begin the evidence, Mr. Stewart has informed that he wishes to take two minutes on a point, and we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And before I give an opportunity to do that - - no, I'll wait with that. The dossiers of Novi Grad and Banja Luka still need to be assigned exhibit numbers, but perhaps Mr. Registrar will wait until Ms. Philpott is back to assist us because she has a better overview. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It was only this briefly, Your Honour: Of course, we have all been - and I think all of us actually, one way or another - have been involved in complicated and not always particularly easy negotiations and discussions over the last two or three weeks, while at the same time all or most of us are having to deal with witnesses who are sometimes complicated and not easy either. Your Honour, the position is this: We are approaching a time that I know that the Trial Chamber had in mind as a time when, really, these matters needed to be concluded one way or another or brought to a head. Your Honour, the -- in view of all the various issues, I and my team, we really do need to have this weekend to think about all these things and pull the threads together. We, on the Defence side, are certainly anxious that this matter should not be left in limbo for much longer, which we believe is a position shared by the Trial Chamber and all concerned and Mr. Krajisnik. What we would ask is that perhaps, if it is convenient and fits the Trial Chamber's planning, that sometime early next week appropriate opportunities might be given for the Defence and everybody else to express their up-to-date views on where we are at the end of this week and at the very beginning of next week. But, Your Honour, I'm just asking that we don't grapple with all these issues before the weekend because we really do need some time to reflect and discuss matters on the Defence side. But then, please, may we have, in the light of -- of where we are, then, may we have appropriate opportunity early next week to make whatever representations, submissions fit in with where everybody is at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, of course, the Chamber will give an opportunity to make such submissions. At the same time, I would say it goes almost without saying that the Chamber is -- of course, was concerned about the situation. The Chamber very much was in favour of resolving the matter between Mr. Krajisnik, the Defence team, and the Registrar. Although the Chamber itself, of course, is not responsible for the composition of the Defence team, it has a task, in this respect, to the extent that these problems would affect the trial, the fairness of the trial, and the rights of the accused. We'll wait until after the weekend, and we'll hear your submissions. Again, the Chamber hopes and is still confident that an agreement can be reached. Of course, if not, then the Chamber will have to decide on a matter which is pending already for a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's understood, Your Honour. And may I ensure Your Honour that I and my team, so far as they are actively involved - though it is mainly me on this one - I will continue over the next couple of days to work to do what I can, but really by close of play on Friday, I suspect that we will know what progress we've made, where we are, and then that reflection and those submissions will ensue. But thank you, Your Honour. That's very cooperative, if I may say so, and we appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the Prosecution has no submissions to make in this respect. Otherwise, I'll hear from them. We'll then, now, still being in open session, but we'll now have the videolink with Sarajevo. And we receive that on -- yes, on video evidence. May I just check with the technicians whether the face distortion and the voice distortion is effective because I can't check that on my screen at this moment. I -- yes, I see on the video screen that at least the face distortion is effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to the representative of the Registry and the witness in Sarajevo. Can you hear me, Witness 031, because that's how I'm going to address you. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So everything is all right. Witness, before you give evidence before this Tribunal, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text, as I see, is now handed out to you by the representative of the Registry. Good morning to you, as well. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 031, protective measures are in effect. That means that no one in the outside world can see your face, can hear your own voice, and we'll not use your own name. We'll address you by the pseudonym 31. You'll now first be examined by Mr. Gaynor, who's here in The Hague, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Gaynor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd request that the registrar show the witness the pseudonym sheet, please. Examined by Mr. Gaynor:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 031, could you confirm that that is your name and that is your date of birth on that sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask my friend just to stop for a moment. There's a problem with my client's translation, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The usher is very helpfully trying to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some technical problems here at this moment, so we'll just have a pause for a short moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my own microphone was on while Mr. Krajisnik's was being sorted out. I apologise. We were having some informal chats here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if that was shared, then it was really not much to do with the case, Your Honour, frankly, but my apologies if that got shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of more importance, I'm afraid Mr. Karganovic is doing something for us at the moment. We perhaps could benefit from him to interpret between the technician and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- first of all, to inform Sarajevo, we are still busy to resolve the technical problem we have with the translation to B/C/S at this very moment. I'll speak a few words so that you, Mr. Krajisnik, can check whether you now get translation on the right channel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't hear a single word that the witness said. That's why I tried to get the technician's help. There are six channels, and the witness should be listened to on channel 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are eight -- there are more than six channels. I do understand that at least the distorted voice of the witness could be heard on channel 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite Sarajevo to ask the witness to speak a few words to see whether what he says is ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been able to follow everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, has the matter been resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can continue. I was just about to ask the witness to make the solemn declaration of which the text was handed out to him. Could I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, Witness, you made that solemn declaration before. When I asked you to do it and to do it again, it was so that Mr. Krajisnik could hear you make that solemn declaration, as well. Mr. Gaynor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the pseudonym sheet, please. Could you confirm that that is your name and your date of birth on that sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes, the details are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to instruct the representative of the Registry in Sarajevo to keep the pseudonym sheet with her as an exhibit, attached to it a brief statement, which could be a one-line statement that this is the pseudonym sheet you received from the witness, and where you received it, when you received it. Take it back to The Hague so that the pseudonym sheet together with this short statement will be admitted as an exhibit, and the number would then be, Mr. Registrar ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit will be tendered and admitted under evidence under the reference P878, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request to go into private session to introduce some details with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request the registrar now to give to the witness his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is that a statement which records interviews you had with members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to carefully review that statement over the past two days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that statement true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Having had a look at the statement, it does correspond to what I said; on the whole, yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'd request that the statement be given an exhibit number, and we tender that statement under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. This piece of -- this document will be tendered into evidence under the reference P879, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to read for the public a summary of the evidence contained in your statement. KRAJ 031 is a Bosnian Muslim from a village in the municipality of Ilijas. In his written statement, the witness states that, prior to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. outbreak of conflict, fuel was removed from a major JNA fuel warehouse in Ilijas municipality. The witness states that local SDS president and president of the municipality, Ratko Adzic, ordered that a permit for the construction of a Catholic church should not be issued. The witness also describes efforts in late 1991 by the SDS deputies in Ilijas Municipal Assembly, led by Ratko Adzic, to pass a resolution in the Municipal Assembly permitting Ilijas municipality to join the SAO Romanija. As the SDS did not have an absolute majority in the Municipal Assembly, the resolution initially did not pass. Under SDS pressure, an SDP Municipal Assembly member was persuaded to vote for the decision. This provided the SDS with the requisite majority, and Ilijas joined the SAO Romanija. Signs at the municipality building were changed accordingly. An SDS flag flew from the municipality building. Non-Serb policemen were disarmed and dismissed. The local SDK branch was taken over, and taxes were paid to the SAO Romanija instead of to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Non-Serbs were unable to cash cheques; non-Serb pensioners no longer received their pensions. Non-Serbs were dismissed from their positions in the TO, the health centre, and the employment bureau. A large fuel facility, belonging to the oil company INA, was taken over by White Eagles and others following the takeover of the municipality. Muslims and Croats who worked at the fuel facility were dismissed. Barricades, manned by local SDS officials, including the president of the Municipality, Ratko Adzic, were set up. Vehicles and people were searched for weapons. The witness overheard Ratko Adzic explain to three young men, who were dissatisfied with the task of carrying out searches, that there would later be opportunities for killing and proving themselves. The witness describes the presence of young men from the Knin front in town. In May 1992, Serb police arrived at the witness's village in an APC. A Serb policeman demanded that the villagers surrender their weapons and recognise that they were living in SAO Romanija. He said that he would provide security for the village after this recognition. The witness left his village on 3rd of June, 1992, and remained in Breza municipality until the end of the war. The witness also describes the destruction of religious and cultural property. All 21 Muslim religious monuments in the municipality of Ilijas were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That ends the reading of the summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to ask you a few questions about your statement. There's no need for you to refer to your statement while I'm doing this. Now, in your statement, as I've just mentioned, you said there were -- this is at paragraph 14 and also at paragraph 15 of the witness's statement. You said that there were 21 religious monuments in the Ilijas municipality, which were of the Bosniak people and Islamic religion. How many of those monuments were mosques?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Out of the 21 Muslim buildings in the Ilijas municipality, three of them were mosques. There were three mosques: One in town; there was one in Srednje, and there was another in Srna Rijeka. The other religious buildings were smaller ones, where religious rites were performed, and there were two buildings in which religious rights weren't performed, but the Muslims used them. The Muslims attached a lot of importance to these buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of the information which you received when you were in Breza municipality, how many of the 21 Muslim religious facilities were destroyed in the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: In 1992, religious facilities were destroyed as certain inhabited places were taken in Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of the 21 which you name in your statement --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: So, for example -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to interrupt. Of the 21 which you -- which you refer to in your statement, how many of those 21 were destroyed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Out of the 21 facilities -- in 1992, 20 were destroyed. There was only one in Srna Rijeka, which was destroyed in 1993 because an attack in that village was launched at a subsequent date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on now to a separate topic, and that is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, could you try to elicit from the witness what the character of the other religious buildings were. He says there were three mosques. And the character of the other ones, not to go through them one by one, but to give us an impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 21 buildings, Witness, you said three were mosques. Can you describe generically what the other 18 were. What was the character of those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: The other religious buildings were low buildings; they were small buildings. They weren't mosques, but they buildings in which religious rites were performed. They had the same importance as mosques, but in terms of their architecture and their size, they did not resemble mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- can you just give me the -- the names that you refer to them in your own language.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Mesdzid, which is something like a small mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right that some of the others were turbe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes, there were two turbes, which were destroyed. A turbe is not a religious building, but it is a building which the Muslims attached importance to. They would visit such buildings, and such buildings had a certain significance for the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm moving now to a separate topic, which is the -- the votes which preceded the December 24th vote in which the Municipal Assembly decided to join the SAO of Romanija. You say in your statement that "Zoran Zagorcic was put under what you describe as physical pressure by the SDS. This is at paragraph 26. Now, without referring to your statement, Witness, can you tell us, how did you become aware that Mr. Zagorcic was put under pressure by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Well, look, I wasn't a great friend of Zoran Zagorcic, but I knew him since he was a local doctor who worked in the clinic in Ilijas. So in a certain sense, he was a public figure in the town itself. As far as this paragraph is concerned, a decision on separating Ilijas and making it part of the Romanija SAO was a subject of discussion in the town, in the municipality of Ilijas. That was the only subject discussed in town because there was nothing more interesting than that subject, so I did not personally speak to Zoran. I couldn't reach him. But his friends and my friends, Serbs and colleagues of mine with whom I worked on a daily basis and I lived with them in the Ilijas municipality, from them I found out that pressure had been exerted on Zoran Zagorcic. Threats had been issued to him. Three or four times he was to go to a session of the municipal counsel, to vote on that decision. As the only doctor of the Serbian people, Zoran was against that decision. He didn't vote at the very beginning. Soon after, the decision was taken on joining Ilijas municipality to SAO Romanija. Zoran Zagorcic left Ilijas; He left Bosnia Herzegovina. I think he went to live in Serbia. I don't know whether he live there is now, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in your statement - this is paragraph 28 - you referred to the takeover of the police station and you say that weapons were taken away from non-Serb policemen, who were forbidden to come to work. What is the source of your information about the takeover of the police station?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) I don't know what sort of session we are in. He provided me with that information. Because after the multiparty elections, the posts in the police were divided. The commander of the police was a Bosniak, a Muslim, whereas the chief of the police was a Serb. So after this decision had been voted, after the Serbian police in the municipality of Ilijas had been formed, all other policemen, the Bosniaks, the Muslims, and the Croats, they were told that they should accept the SAO and they should work in the Serbian police, and those who did not accept this had to surrender their weapons and leave the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, for your own information --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I obtained this information --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please finish what you were saying, Witness. You obtained this information ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, the witness expressed some concern as to the source and mentioning names. I take it that at the same time he gave some information of which I thought it should be redacted; I gave instructions to do that. At the same time, I'd like you to keep in mind whenever a witness expresses such concerns, that you take the necessary initiative to see that the witness does not testify in open session a matter without further discussion if he has some hesitation to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we are in open session. If there is any information which you wish to provide which you would prefer to provide in private session, please let us know, and then we can go -- I can request that we go into private session. I'll -- I'll move on to a separate topic, Witness, and that is the fuel warehouses. Now, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll refer Your Honours to paragraphs 29 and 31.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to clarify the location of these fuel warehouses. You refer to a JNA fuel warehouse. Where in Ilijas municipality was the JNA fuel warehouse located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It appears we're not receiving interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One belonged to the Zagreb industry of oil in Podlugovi. This was a state warehouse. And the other warehouse of the former JNA in Misoca. And those were the stocks of fuel that belonged to the army, to the Yugoslav People's Army. After the establishment and after the passing of the decision by the Serbian Autonomous Region in Ilijas on the establishment of the Serbian police, the Crisis Staff of Ilijas, headed by the then-president of the Municipality of Ilijas and the president of the Crisis Staff, Ratko Adzic, who was also the president of the Serbian Democratic Party of Ilijas, made a decision on taking both of these warehouses. Let me explain what I mean by the taking of the INA warehouse. The INA warehouse was a civilian and a state warehouse. The workers who worked there who were non-Serbs, Muslims, and Croats were told that they could no longer work for that company and that they should go home. This warehouse was thus taken by the members of the Serbian police from Ilijas, who from then on controlled the movements through that warehouse. They put their inscriptions and marks on that warehouse, so as you walked through the streets, you could see that their -- this was a Serbian warehouse with the Serbian police in it. As for the commodities that had been stored there, it was the Crisis Staff that had taken over that role, the Crisis Staff headed by Ratko Adzic. Every morning when we -- when I came to work, day in, day out I would feel -- I would see lorries with Belgrade, Nis, and Zrenjanin registration plates that drove off fuel from the barracks to Misoca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just want to clarify the locations, and correct me if I'm wrong, but is it right that the JNA fuel facility was in Misoca and the INA fuel facility was in Podlugovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the answer you gave a moment ago, you stated that it was a decision of the Crisis Staff -- it was a decision of Ratko Adzic to take over both of those warehouses. What is it that makes you conclude that it was a decision of Ratko Adzic to take over both of those warehouses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I've concluded that because at that time Ratko Adzic was the most important figure in the municipality of Ilijas. He was the president of the municipality. He was the president of the Crisis Staff. He was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party. He had a reputation, and he enjoyed authority amongst his men who came to him and listened to his orders and obeyed his orders. I never saw a document to that effect; however, I assume that he was the only one who could have passed that decision. I believe that as far as the distribution of fuel from the barracks is concerned, I believe that this was done in agreement with the military bodies. They just went into the barracks freely; they left the barracks freely. They would drive the fuel off. Nobody prevented them from doing that. Only they could do that; it could not be done by any other civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move now to another topic. This is at paragraph 32. In paragraph 32, you referred to the takeover of the SDK, and you say that following the takeover, taxes were paid to the SAO Romanija instead of to the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. How did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreter please ask the Prosecutor to switch their microphone off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is only logical. If the Crisis Staff, headed by Ratko Adzic, in agreement or on the order of the higher bodies of the SDS issued a political decision, such a political decision to be implemented in practice has to be funded. It is in this way that they took over the SDK. This is where all the taxes were being paid on behalf of the SAO Romanija. And they also took over the two commercial banks, the Privredna Bank and the Belgrade Bank that operated in Ilijas and where people banked in Ilijas. Based on this information, everybody could conclude that anybody who came to the SDK to pay any bills, that these bills were paid into their account. That is something that was not difficult to conclude. Ilijas is a very small town; it is not a big city. At that time, people communicated normally; they cooperated. I had friends amongst the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, and in conversations with them I would obtain information, and those were just normal conversations. At that time, a lot of big things happened in Ilijas --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd just like to interrupt briefly, Witness. Did you personally deal with the SDK, either on your own behalf or on behalf of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: As a citizen, on my own behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you bank at Privredna Bank yourself? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes. I banked with Privredna Banka, with its Ilijas branch office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 33 of your statement, you say that -- you suggest that non-Serbs could not cash a cheque at a bank. Now, did you personally attempt to cash any cheques at the Privredna Bank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: We have to put this into a somewhat broader perspective. The CEO of the Privredna Banka at the time was Ratko Karcoca [phoen]. He was also a member of the Crisis Staff, which had been established by Ratko Adzic. In that Crisis Staff, the members were all the people who occupied prominent positions. Ratko received orders from Ratko Adzic. There was a Serbian policeman standing in front of the bank, and the only people who could withdraw their salaries from the bank were the Serbs. The Croats and the Muslims could stand in queues, but they could never get in. It so happened that I had a lot of cheques. I did not have to go to the bank; I could use my cheques to pay for the services in shops or at petrol stations. However, on one or two occasions, I was not able to withdraw my salary from the bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just briefly explain who was preventing you from withdrawing your salary from the bank.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: We were not allowed to enter the bank physically by the Serbian policemen who were standing in front of the bank. That's the physical act. And the decision that was issued and the order that was given to the bank probably came from the Crisis Staff, to the effect that only certain people could withdraw money from the bank; only the Serbs. We were physically prevented by the policemen, who would take your ID and who would tell you, You will not be able to withdraw any money today; you can turn around and go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just moving back to the SDK. Do you know who the director of the Ilijas branch of SDK was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: The director of the branch office in Ilijas was Veljko Kravljaca of the SDK, and the director of the Privredna Banka in Ilijas was Ratko Karcoca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Karcoca was a member of the Ilijas Crisis Staff. Do you know whether the director of the SDK was also a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was. I said all the prominent people in the municipality who occupied important positions -- for example, the chief of MUP, the deputy commander of the Territorial Defence, the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, the director of the SDK, the directors of the banks and all the CEOs of Serb ethnicity in companies who could have contributed towards the implementation of the policies that were in place, the policies that were against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm moving, now, to paragraph 38. I'd like you to clarify a reference you have, Witness, and I'll read out the relevant sentence. You said, "When the Serb police exclusively occupied the police station in Ilijas, they issued an order for Muslims, Croats, and others could no longer work in the police force, in National Defence, in the TO headquarters, in the health centre in Ilijas, and in the employment bureau." There are two issues I'd like you to clarify in relation to that. The suggestion in that sentence is that the police issued an order that non-Serbs could not work in the TO, the health centre, and the employment bureau. Is that, in fact, what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: No, not really. What I wanted to say is this: For every position -- for example, in the police, if a decision of the Crisis Staff was to be implemented, the chief of the police was in charge. In the health centre, it was the director of the health centre who was in charge. He was also a Serb. In the employment bureau, I don't know who it was, but I only know that no Bosniaks could work there any longer. There was a blanket order covering all the institutions that was implemented by the heads of the institutions. I can't say that it was the police who issued those orders. The police only carried out the orders issued by the Crisis Staff to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that same sentence I read out a minute ago, there's a reference to the National Defence and the TO headquarters. Now, when you said "National Defence," did you, in fact, mean to say "Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: In the former Socialist system, the organisation of work was the following: There was a Secretariat for National Defence, which kept various records, the records of material, technical equipment, and recruits. On the other hand, there was the Territorial Defence and its staff; this was the body that managed the material and equipment that belonged to the reserve forces. In both of these bodies, Muslims could no longer work there because both institutions were directly linked to the military formations. In the Territorial Defence, the person in charge of the depot, who was a Croat, had a close shave. He barely survived when they decided to remove him from his job, when they decided to remove him from being in charge of the military depot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to move on to another issue. In paragraph 39 at -- on the second line on page 8 of the statement - that's in English - Witness, you refer -- you're referring to the period May 1992, and you say that you still had TV, radio, and telephone and had word of takeovers across the country. First of all, which radio station did you -- was serving the municipality of Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Ilijas is in the place where we could receive all radio and TV stations. We also had our local radio, the Radio of Ilijas. When the Serbian Municipality of Ilijas, it became the Serbian Radio of Ilijas. We received a local information, the information that was relative to the work and life in Ilijas, from our own local radio, which was the radio of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the takeover of Radio Ilijas, were any non-Serbs employed by Radio Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lady; she was in charge of music or something like that. However, when this became the Serbian Radio of Ilijas, this lady was fired and she no longer came to work. I suppose that her lot was the same as the lot of the workers in the health centre, in the police, in the employment bureau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like you to tell us: Do you know who the director of Radio Ilijas was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: The director of that radio station was Vlado Markanovic. Interestingly enough, when Radio Ilijas became the Serbian Radio of Ilijas, the music it played, the news it aired changed to suit the needs of the Serbian Democratic Party. I knew Vlado very well. He put up a certain degree of resistance to those radical changes and to the emphasis of all things national on Radio Ilijas, on -- to the propaganda in the media. Vlado Markanovic, unfortunately, did not stay long at the radio after that. I'm not going to say that he was fired. I only know that he left the radio station, he left the town of Ilijas, and I think he went to Novi Sad. And as far as I know, he is still there; he still resides there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who succeeded Vlado Markanovic as director of Serbian Radio Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: While Vlado Markanovic was director, he had his, so to say, portparole. That was the man who was the portparole of the Crisis Staff and the SDS. He was Mirko Ostojic. I don't know whether he was director of Radio Ilijas, but it was his voice that we heard most often. He was the one who provided us with information, instructions. He was the one who emphasised the national content of Radio Ilijas. That's why I'm saying that he was the spokesman for the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in an earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I saw the witness was looking at some document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think it was his statement. Could we perhaps inquire what it is, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness 031, could I ask you: We just saw you on the screen having a document in your hands. Was that your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my statement before me, and I also have the transcripts that I used to prepare myself. And if you want to know, I also have excerpts from the book that was written after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its author is Mr. Veljo Adzic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I invite you to put aside everything apart from your statement. And if there's any need to consult any of the other documents you have in front of you, please ask permission to do so. And may I ask you: Have you consulted these other documents during the testimony you are giving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should be aware of the fact that during the war I had a work obligation. I was not a member of the army. I was in charge of keeping the record of the situation that prevailed in Ilijas. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this record that I kept -- yes. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to interrupt you. Whatever information you have, the Chamber wants to know exactly when you answer questions with consulting documents or without consulting documents. You are expected to answer the question without consulting any documents unless you specifically ask permission for that. Could you please answer the question I just put to you, is that whether until now you have consulted any of these documents, apart from your own statement given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the statement that I gave to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would feel any need to consult any of the other documents that are not in front of you anymore at this moment, could you please address me and ask permission to do so. You may proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, a couple of minutes ago, in relation to the answer which you gave about Serb Radio Ilijas, you referred to propaganda and you said that the radio station was being used to serve SDS needs. Now, could you give us a few examples of the kind of messages which you heard on Serb Radio Ilijas, which you would consider to -- to be propaganda.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Radio Ilijas was a well-known radio station for its musical content. The first change that we could notice was in the musical content of that radio station. All of a sudden we could hear songs that belonged to the national body of the Serbian people. Secondly, the information that came from Mirko Ostojic were nationalistic and filled with tensions. When I say that, I mean he would say, If there was an attack against Ilijas by the extremists, Islamic extremists, the Green Berets, the HOS, and so on and so forth. On Radio Ilijas, you could hear nothing but this charge that was in the air that prepared the Serbian people for something that would happen later. It was preparing the Serbs to all root for that one Serbian cause. The information that we heard on the Serbian Radio Ilijas was also the topical information; for example, whether there was water, electricity, whether the phones were working, what the situation in the town was like. Very often Radio Ilijas also had conferences that were held between the neighbouring municipalities, the Breza municipality, the municipality of Ilijas, and the heads of the municipalities often spoke about different things, and Radio Ilijas very often reported from these conferences that took place in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a few examples of how the Serbs -- sorry, I'll restate that -- how the Muslims and Croats were referred to on Serb Radio Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Muslim extremists and Croatian HOS members, HOS members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd request that we go into private session for a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we are close to a break. But before we have a break, and after the break, you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence, I'd like to ask one question to you in relation to the mosques. You said there were three mosques. Could you be a bit more precise on where these mosques were located in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. One of the mosques was in Stari Ilijas. It was called the "town mosque" because in the very centre of Ilijas, there were no mosques. This was the main, central mosque for Ilijas, and it was located in Stari Ilijas. The second mosque was in Srednje, which is a small place. It's smaller than the town of Ilijas. So as I have said, it was in Srednje. And the third mosque was located in Srna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would mention a mosque in Misoca, could you relate that to any of the mosques you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the mosque in Misoca, at the very beginning of the attack on Misoca, it was destroyed; perhaps I forgot to mention it. But it had more or less the same religious importance as all the other mosques that I have mentioned. It was really in the centre of the area of combat, and it was razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any knowledge whether this was a result of normal combat activity or whether this was the result of a specific attack on that building as a religious building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the building was destroyed for the same reason that all other religious Islamic buildings were destroyed; it had no strategic importance for the army. That wasn't why it was destroyed. It was destroyed for the simple reason that it was a religious building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were the buildings surrounding the mosque in Misoca, were they also destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything was destroyed. As far as Misoca is concerned, the place was entirely destroyed. Not a single building, not a single house remained intact. And I'm referring to Misoca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you whether any of the religious buildings you earlier mentioned was located in Bioca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a mesdzid in -- in Bioca, which was also destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I would mention a mosque in Ilijas without any further specification, could you relate that to any of the mosques you have mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And which one would that be? Could you give a further -- of course, I do understand that all the mosques you mentioned were in the municipality of Ilijas. But if I would just say "mosque in Ilijas," which one would you think of, or would you think -- could you not ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd only think of the mosque in Stari Ilijas because in the new part of the town of Ilijas there was no mosque. That part of the population, the population from the new part of Ilijas, used the mosque located in Stari Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. We'll have a break now until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 031, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Josse, representing the accused. Cross-examined by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, firstly, let me say this. If there's any question that I ask you that requires the Tribunal or the Chamber to go into private session, just say, please. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the book that you were looking at in the course of the questions that you were asked by prosecuting counsel. You say it was a book by someone called Veljko Adzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the book called, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: The book is called "Isijas Nemanijici."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it deal with, in broad terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: The book was written after the end of the war. Veljko Adzic wrote it. He's a relative of Ratko Adzic; he was close to him. The book is about the situation in the territory of Ilijas municipality before the free elections, after the free elections, and it is about the appointment of the Crisis Staff, about the decision on proclaiming the existence of the SAO Romanija, and it is also about the liberation, in inverted commas, of villages and inhabited places by the Serbian army. In the second part of the book, reference is made to military formations about the composition of the Serbian Ilijas Brigade. It deals with Serbian combatants who were killed, who were cited. The book was approved of by the commanders of the Serbian Ilijas brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I can understand you having read the book, but why did you feel it necessary to take it with you into the room where you're giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Well, I analysed my transcripts and information on the book and information in the book -- information that is in the book and in my transcripts, information that I have. All this information tallies, as far as the dates are concerned. In order to be aware of how the other side thinks, it's necessary to read books written by someone from the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, for the purpose of your evidence, do you need to understand how the other side thinks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Well, I understand how the other side thinks. I've understood this from the very beginning, so it's not really necessary for me to remind myself of this. The information concerned is purely technical. It concerns the first and last names of individuals and dates and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why actually have the book physically with you at the point you're giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Well, I usually carry this book with me, and I study it, and I think about it. I think about what the writer wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago your transcripts. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said, and I quote, "I analysed my transcripts and information on the book and information the book -- information that is in the book and in my transcripts, information that I have." So in the sentence that I've just quoted to you, you twice talk about "my transcripts". Are you referring to your witness statement, or are you referring to some other document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: My statement as a witness is also my transcript -- the transcripts that I made, that I wrote for a number of years. I could not bring them here because there are a lot of papers, a lot of information. Some of this information I keep in my head; some of the information I put on paper. I don't know whether I have provided you with a precise enough answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have. The last question, I think, on this topic: What actually did you bring into the room with you this morning in Sarajevo? In Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other words, which documents? We know you've got the book by Mr. Adzic. We know you've got your witness statement there. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I have my diary with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your personal diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's your diary from 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: No. That is a diary that has nothing to do with any particular year. These are just my notes, my reminders, the things that I wrote to remind myself of some things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm going to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have one question, additional question in this respect. Witness 031 when you gave your statement in 1997, had you at that time already read the book you just mentioned by -- of which the author is Mr. Adzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not get hold of the book at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next subject I want to ask you about is the lead-up to the war in Ilijas. Now, is it right that after war had broken out in Croatia in the summer of 1991, the Bosniaks in Ilijas began to arm themselves secretly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I don't know where the Bosniaks could have obtained arms from. They could only have purchased arms from the Serbs, through private channels. Things like that happened because the Serbs had been issued with weapons free of charge; whereas, the Muslims, on the other hand, if they wanted to obtain weapons, they had to purchase weapons. There were such Serbs who had a surplus of weapons, I suppose, and decided to sell the surplus. During that period of time, none of the sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina were well off. Nobody had too much money. So that people who had the needs to purchase weapons did that individually through their own private channels; whereas, the Serbs were issued with weapons collectively by the Serbian Democratic Party or with the help of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you began the answer to the question I've just asked you by saying, "I am not aware of that," and you've then gone on to describe ways in which Muslims may have obtained arms. Do you have any knowledge at all of Muslims arming themselves in 1991 after the outbreak of the Croatian war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Sir, your question was whether the Muslims did that. I don't know -- or actually, I know that they did not have the funds to be armed on a large scale. What I spoke about were some individual cases, some sporadic cases when you compare them to the Serbian people who had obtained weapons from the former JNA with the help of the SDS. There's no comparison between the two cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't seeking to make any comparisons. I was simply asking a -- a question about arms. And let me ask you another question: Have you heard of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Of course I did. On TV, in the media. I read in the newspapers. Just like I did about the Serbian Democratic Party and the armed forces of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to instruct you in the following way: When you were asked about whether you know anything about Bosniaks arming themselves, you tend to compare that with other situations. I'd like to instruct you to answer the questions. If there would be any need to know how Serbs did arm themselves - and the Chamber has heard quite some evidence on that - you'll certainly be asked about it, and then you may address that matter. But it's not up to you to constantly make that comparison. So please answer the questions of Mr. Josse. And, Mr. Josse, when you asked the witness whether he knew about the Bosniaks arming themselves, the witness correctly made a distinction between collective arming and individual arming, and that's how the Chamber understood his answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, Witness, I'm asking you about arming in the Ilijas municipality. I've already said at the -- in 1991. I've asked you about the Patriotic League. By the same token, you've obviously heard of the Green Berets, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I have to go back to my previous answer. Sir, I never heard of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League in Ilijas. I did hear of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets in the city of Sarajevo. At that time, the municipality of Ilijas had already been blocked. There were barricades around it; there were armed guards around it. In my view, no contact whatsoever was possible with those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to 1992. As far as you were concerned, how did hostilities begin in the Ilijas municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: This is a direct question; I'll provide you with a direct answer. In my view and according to my information, the conflict in Ilijas was caused by the Serbian forces. They had attempted an attack across Ilijas, or rather, Odzak, towards the municipality of Breza. They intended to take the coal mine there. According to my information, during that attack, with the help of the village guards and later on the police in Breza, this attack was successfully repelled. After that, the Serbian armed forces in the municipality of Ilijas started launching attacks against non-Serbian population in various settled areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you say that initial Serb attack took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the date or the period of time, but I believe that this was in May, maybe at the beginning of May. In any case, before the massacre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the place of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask whether Mr. Josse is going to ask a question, whether he's going to seek clarification as to what he meant when he said "the Serb forces." The witness said, "[In English] In my view and according to my information, the conflict in Ilijas was caused by the Serbian forces." I would like the witness to clarify what he meant by "the Serb forces." What was the reference being made there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time -- at that time, the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Ilijas had the Serb police, and it also had some voluntary forces which were deployed in villages to keep village guards. They were well armed, they wore camouflage uniforms, and they used military vehicles, some of them. Some of the members of the volunteers wore camouflage uniforms; whereas, some others wore the uniforms of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to suggest that you're right, that fighting broke out in early May of 1992. I want to suggest that on the 3rd of May of that year it was Muslim forces that attacked Serb forces in Ilijas from Visoko and Breza; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: That is your opinion that I cannot subscribe to, and I believe that you are not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of the fighting, I want to suggest that Serbian refugees arrived in May of 1992 in Ilijas. Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes. Serb refugees did come to Ilijas from the municipalities that you mentioned; that is correct. However, those people had been ordered by the Serbian Democratic Party to abandon those places, that there was no way to defend them because they were a minority in those municipalities, just like the Muslims and Croats were in Ilijas. And it is true that the Serbs from the municipalities that you mentioned abandoned their villages, but they were not expelled from their villages. Just for your information, let me tell you this: After a decision of the SAO Romanija was issued, the municipality of Ilijas and its marginal areas, Visoko, Breza, and Vares, where the majority of the population was Serb population, were forcefully merged with the Serbian Municipality of Ilijas. In other words, the suburbs of Ilijas were forcibly merged with the Serbian Municipality of Ilijas without the prior consent of any other municipalities in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not going to spend too long dealing with the demographics of the area before the war, but it's right, isn't it, that in Ilijas, as your statement makes clear, there was just a -- well, Serbs were just the most numerous ethnic group within the municipality, followed very closely by Muslims. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also correct that the surrounding areas, the areas surrounding the municipality, were, as you've just told us, predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Are you referring to the municipality of Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Partly yes, but partly no. Not only Muslims lived in the peripheral parts of the municipality of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The refugees that arrived in May of 1992, can you put any figure on how many there were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Are you referring to the refugees that I received in Breza?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serbian refugees who arrived in Ilijas in May of 1992. You -- you hadn't gone to Breza by that time, had you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Sir, I was not in Ilijas at the time. I did not reside in the urban part of Ilijas. I was on the periphery. There were very few Muslims in Ilijas at the time, and hardly anybody can tell you how many Serbs, how many Serb refugees there were in Ilijas. And although they were in Ilijas, they did not have a good receipt there; they were not well received there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I could ask you various questions about what happened thereafter in the municipality - that's in June - but as you've told us, you left in early June to go to Breza, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware the activities of Muslim forces in Breza preparing for further attacks on Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: No. There was no way for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you follow the progress of the war in Ilijas from Breza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it may be an obvious question, but how did you do that? Through the media, firsthand reports from people who were fighting? Tell us how you found out what was going on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: This is how I followed it: All the civilians that had been expelled from the villages and the urban part of Ilijas I received as refugees, as displaced persons. Initially, I provided them with initial aid. I helped them find accommodation, I helped them seek medical attention, and, also, I talked to them. In addition to that, of course, Radio Ilijas worked; the state television of Bosnia-Herzegovina worked; the state radio of Bosnia- Herzegovina worked. The Serbian television called SRNA was also operational. The media of Bosnia and Herzegovina, each and every one in their own way, conveyed information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll put one specific thing to you: At paragraph 44 of your witness statement, you referred to a Serb policeman called Radenko Markovic. Do you know what happened to Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me find that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, would you like to -- when he says, "Just a moment. Let me find that," do you want him to consult any ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy for him to read paragraph 44, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh he's -- yes, he's finding the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought he was trying to find the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was looking for this passage, number 44, Your Honour. Markovic was in Ljesevo, and he did provide a guarantee the way it's described here. But on the 5th of June he was also there. I'm sure that you have this book, "The Nemanjici of Ilijas." There Veljko Adzic wrote that he had been killed that afternoon. It is from this book that I learned he was killed. I personally know him, and I know for a fact that he was in Ljesevo on the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My instructions are that he was, in fact, killed in late June of 1992 in, we think - and again, excuse my pronunciation - a place called Misoca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I don't have that information. There was no way for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just deal with it like this: You've told us you knew Radenko Markovic before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Yes, only superficially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you haven't seen him since, have you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Not personally, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be best to go into private session next. I want to ask about a topic -- I've discussed with Mr. Gaynor, and we thought it best that we should ask the witness if it's a matter of sensitivity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you may proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Krajisnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please just tell me when the third session was held at which the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija was proclaimed -- or rather, when did Ilijas become part of that region? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: That is contained in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you please answer the question and provide us with a date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Well, if you want the precise date ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't exactly know what the point of this question is. The evidence is before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 24, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I put a simple question to the witness. He ought to know the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whether he ought to know is a different matter, but you can ask him the question, and 24 does not give an answer to the question, Mr. Gaynor. It gives an answer to the question when a request was submitted. And the question was not when the request was submitted but when Ilijas joined, and that's not exactly the same, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- I accept your point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, could you tell us when Ilijas joined the -- decided to join the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilijas wanted to join the Romanija SAO from the very beginning. The Serbian Democratic Party was organised in such a way to have a government in the SAO, and in my testimony, I said this was on the 24th of December, 1991, at a session of the council. So I don't know what else I could add.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was - because in your statement, it becomes clear that not at the first vote that the request was accepted - were those votes on the same day or on the 24th of December, or were the second and third round on later dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was later. It wasn't all on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a seven-to-ten-day period between these two events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when finally was the decision adopted that Ilijas would become part of the Serbian Autonomous Region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it says the 24th of December, 1991, in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your statement - and I'll read that to you - is "So SDS deputies, headed by Ratko Adzic, submitted a request at the Assembly session on December 24th, 1991, to include the municipality of Ilijas into the so-called SAO Romanija." If you say that finally this decision was adopted at another session, then it could not be on the 24th of December. So again I ask you whether you remember when, finally, the decision was adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the final decision was adopted on the 24th of December, 1991. Perhaps there was a mistranslation -- or I wouldn't say "mistranslation," but the idea had been mentioned earlier on. And on the 24th of December, this decision was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Krajisnik, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you said that the police force was divided. Could you tell us when this happened -- or rather, when was the Serbian police in Ilijas established after that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say that the police force divided -- became divided. I said that it was restructured. The term "the Serbian police of Ilijas" was added -- the term "Serbian" was added, but the other members of the police, the Bosniaks and the Croats, stopped going to work; they did not continue to work in the police station. So this is quite different. You are trying to say that the Muslims had their police force. As far as I am aware, they did not have their own police force. But perhaps you have information according to which they did have such a force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't think that they had their own police force. All I wanted to know was the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it takes some time until the translation reaches us, so would you please make a pause. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We both speak the same language, although some call it the Bosnian language and others the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I continue immediately, it doesn't mean that I have any doubts about your answers. All I'm interested in is when this decision was taken. So after the 24th, when Ilijas joined the SAO, when was the police transformed into the Serbian police, as you put it? If you could pause briefly, and then answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Has it been interpreted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: Thank you. As you put it, we do speak the same language, so we can understand each other immediately. You know that after the decision was taken to form the Romanija SAO, all the institutions in all the municipalities, not only in Ilijas - there's also the municipality of Han Pijesak, et cetera - they were all given the prefix "Serbian" and soon afterwards - I don't know the exact date - a lot of time has passed since then, so I can't provide you with the exact date. That date did not concern me directly, so I can't tell you the exact date - but after the political decision was taken on the organisation of Ilijas municipality, after that point in time, all the other institutions were organised at this level and this way. They were given a "Serbian" prefix. They became Serbian institutions, and things then unfolded in the way that they unfolded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one say that it was in January or perhaps a little earlier? You don't have to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: I'll just wait for the interpretation to finish. I think it was fairly soon afterwards, maybe in February or March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the second answer. If you say "soon afterwards," could you be more precise. When was the police force transformed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 031
utterances.text: From the 24th of December onwards. The month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you please put your next question to the witness. This matter, as far as the date is concerned, has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have done that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd just like to say, well, thank you for that, Your Honour. The -- the practical matter is I feel that Mr. Josse and I would simply like to make sure we have ample opportunity over this break to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to make whatever inquiries -- which may not take very long at all, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break, anyhow, for half an hour because that's the time needed to get the courtroom in the normal order again. If, during the next half an hour, you would fail to receive the information you would need or if one of you would fail to receive the information you would need under those circumstances, please inform the Chamber so that we can see how we can accommodate your needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Your Honour. It seems doubtful that more than that half-an-hour break will be needed, anyway. But thank you for that, and we will keep everybody informed, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just a minor procedural matter. Not necessarily now. But I'd request that the two exhibits be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They are -- I heard no objections. Therefore, they are admitted into evidence. We'll have a break now until 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I hope, Mr. Stewart, Mr. Josse, that whatever information you could get is not any more alarming than the general information that reaches us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. In fact, from our entirely personal point of view, Your Honour, we're -- we're happy to have established that everybody concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- is safe. It doesn't help anybody else. We understand that. But at least we're here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope also that this caused the Chamber again to wait not just one or two minutes but even more before we could start. And I am aware that now and then those in this courtroom have to wait for the Chamber, but the balance seems to go now the other way, which should not be, for the future, the rule. Then are you -- we now turn into closed session for the continuation of the examination of Witness 666.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of July, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
